summary: Describes Hybrid Public Key Encryption, a way to encrypt data of any size to a recipient's public key. It combines a key encapsulation mechanism, a key derivation function, and an authenticated encryption algorithm, and includes authenticated variants. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: HPKE lets a sender encrypt data so that only the holder of a recipient's private key can decrypt it. It combines public-key methods to set up a secret with faster encryption for the messages themselves.

questions: how does hybrid public key encryption work
how does hpke differ from ecies
subtitle: A recipe for encrypting messages to a recipient's public key using three cryptographic building blocks.

tldr.problem: Hybrid public-key encryption schemes had competing designs and could be difficult to implement interoperably. RFC 9180 specifies one construction from public-key and symmetric cryptography.
tldr.mechanism: A key encapsulation mechanism creates a shared secret for the recipient, a key derivation function turns it into keys, and authenticated encryption protects messages. Four modes vary whether a pre-shared key or sender key is also used.
tldr.outcome: HPKE is a low-level building block, not a complete message protocol. Applications must define message encoding, ordering, replay protection, and downgrade protection.

today: RFC 9180 is an Informational document. The unit metadata lists no updates or replacement RFCs.

sections.title: The Goal of Hybrid Encryption
sections.content:
Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) encrypts plaintext of any size for a recipient's public key. The sender creates an encapsulated shared secret and uses it to encrypt one or more messages. The recipient uses the matching private key to recover the secret and decrypt the messages.

Hybrid encryption combines public-key techniques for key setup with symmetric encryption for data. RFC 9180 defines a construction intended to make implementations interoperable. It also describes authenticated variants that can show the sender holds a pre-shared key or a KEM private key.
sections.plainLanguage: HPKE uses the recipient's public key to set up a secret, then uses that secret to encrypt the message. The public-key step handles setup, while the message is protected with symmetric encryption.

sections.title: The Three Cryptographic Building Blocks
sections.content:
A key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) creates a shared secret and an encapsulated value that the recipient can open with its private key. A key derivation function (KDF) uses that secret and other inputs to produce key material. An authenticated encryption with associated data algorithm (AEAD) encrypts the message and checks that it was not changed.

A ciphersuite selects one KEM, one KDF, and one AEAD. The RFC defines Diffie-Hellman-based KEMs and lists initial algorithm identifiers. The KDF inputs include labels that separate HPKE's uses of the derivation function.
sections.plainLanguage: HPKE has three parts: one sets up a shared secret, one derives keys from it, and one encrypts and checks each message. Both sides need to use the same set of algorithms.

sections.title: Modes and Encryption Contexts
sections.content:
Every mode first creates an encryption context shared by sender and recipient. The base mode uses the recipient's public key alone. The PSK mode also uses a pre-shared key; the Auth mode uses the sender's KEM key pair; AuthPSK combines both additions. A KEM that lacks authenticated operations cannot support the Auth modes.

The context holds an AEAD key, a base nonce, a sequence number, and an exporter secret. Each message uses a nonce derived from the base nonce and the sequence number, which advances after each operation. The sequence number starts at zero, and the implementation must fail if it overflows. The sender encrypts and the recipient decrypts; the same context is not bidirectional.

The RFC also gives single-shot interfaces for the common case of encrypting or decrypting one message, and an interface for deriving additional secrets from a context.
sections.plainLanguage: The four modes add different kinds of proof to the basic setup: a shared secret, a sender key, both, or neither. Once setup is complete, each message uses the next number in the context to get a fresh nonce.

sections.title: Algorithm Choices and Identifiers
sections.content:
RFC 9180 assigns identifiers to KEMs, KDFs, and AEADs. Its initial KEM choices use P-256, P-384, P-521, X25519, or X448 with HKDF. The KDF choices are HKDF-SHA256, HKDF-SHA384, and HKDF-SHA512. The AEAD choices are AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, and ChaCha20Poly1305.

Applications choose a compatible combination. The RFC recommends limiting application-provided values such as info, psk, and psk_id to 64 bytes to support implementations that allocate fixed-size memory. Future specifications may add algorithms that meet the RFC's security requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications choose one supported algorithm for each of HPKE's three parts. Short identifiers let the sender and recipient agree on those choices.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limits
sections.content:
The RFC describes message secrecy and sender authentication goals for the modes that provide authentication. Its security analysis assumes the underlying cryptographic algorithms meet their stated requirements. The Auth modes based on the defined DHKEMs have a key-compromise impersonation limitation.

HPKE does not provide application-level message ordering, replay protection, downgrade prevention, or plaintext-length hiding. If the recipient's long-term private key is compromised, earlier ciphertexts may be decrypted. Applications must define how they transport the encapsulated value and ciphertexts and how they handle loss or reordering.
sections.plainLanguage: HPKE encrypts messages, but it does not handle every risk around sending them. The application must protect message order and replay, and a stolen recipient private key can expose earlier messages.

references.text: Rescorla, E., "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3", RFC 8446.
